utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. You may have heard that in order to avoid that the witness has to come a second time to The Hague, we have additional time. But this shouldn't be an invitation to be as long as we all have been with the last witness. I think we should all speak aloud mea culpa related to the last witness. I think we, all of us, could have been shorter. So let's try -- what is your real estimate the time you would need.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Approximately an hour and a half to two hours, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then let's try to do it in one session, and then the cross the same period in time. And in case we all show the necessary self-restraint, then it will be in good time. I want to let you know that next week on Wednesday, exceptionally we sit in the morning instead of the afternoon. There was a change necessary because of an extraordinary bureau meeting which is now unfortunately rescheduled for Thursday. This means that on Thursday, we have to start a little bit later. As regards all the other changes in the schedule in the future, I'll let you know as soon as possible. Only that you know for those of you who want to leave The Hague, everybody should know that we hear this case the 7th of February. But in exchange, the day between UN holiday and the day between court recess will be a day without any hearing. So this means from Wednesday to Friday, no hearing that week. But you'll get it in writing as soon as possible. Without further ado, may I ask the usher to bring in the witness. May I hear any change as regards protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, there is no change in connection with that issue, Your Honour, but I would like to make an oral application of a different kind if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: As the Court has reviewed our proffer, we would like to add to our proffer an issue that Mrs. Kovacevic will be discussing, and that is her employment. As I do with most witness cover their employment history. She will share with us information and data she has received in connection with refugees who were coming to the Prijedor municipality from 1991 through 1995. We would ask that be allowed to be inquired of, and we also brought the documentation in CD form, and we would like for her to explain, at least in part, some of that documentation the headings, et cetera. And I think subsequent to that it should be self-explanatory for all of us to read. Because there are listings of names, addresses, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, after reviewing that material, we may ask for additional time to review it and cross-examine the witness. What we had until this moment is a three-sentence summary of this witness's testimony. And to have -- a moment before she testifies have it be disclosed that there's going to be a CD admitted into evidence with her testimony, which I understand is not part of the Defence exhibit list, we think we are entitled if -- depending on what it is, to additional time before we complete our cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We are also taken by surprise. The witness has testified beforehand in this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge, Your Honour, she has not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So the content of this CD will be in concreto what?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The CD will help establish, we think, and rebut certain allegations made in the fourth amended complaint, specifically relating to the population in the Prijedor municipality and the events pre-, during, and post-April through September of 1992. We believe that it addresses specifically issues of various witnesses offered by the OTP, specifically Mr. Robert Donia, Dr. Ewa Tabeau, and several of the lay witnesses who testified about various exodus and movement of people within that region at that time. We also believe that it specifically goes to count 7 and 8 of the fourth amended indictment, which we think can help establish certain factors and assist the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask why it was not possible to present this CD beforehand?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. The explanation is we recently received the CD Your Honour. And immediately upon receiving the CD, we had to examine it as well, unlike -- and respectfully, unlike the OTP witnesses, we do not have an opportunity to meet with our witnesses years and months in advance. We are literally meeting our witnesses for the first time when they arrive at The Hague. And she brought this CD with her. And it was at that time, after we reviewed it, that we thought it was be prudent to produce that CD. We think it's important. We certainly think it's most relevant --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. The picture becomes more clear. If it's a CD she brought with her, we have had this in the past that a witness brings some evidence. Let's wait and see what and not discuss in the fork when we don't know what it's all about. Let's start hearing the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We have the CD here if the Court would like us to distribute it and to mark it for the Court. I think we previous --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We can play it with our LiveNote laptops?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We have coordinated with the video technicians that we can at least, by way of a sample, go over a couple of pages so the Court can understand various columns that were within the CD. If necessary and if the Court wishes, you can ask her if there's any questions that may immediately come to mind any further. But I think it's really just a listing of individuals with their address, the place where they were from, where they left to, and the year in which they approximately came or specifically to the Prijedor Municipality and when it was reported, their status.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So this CD will be provisionally marked as D43, because D43, unfortunately, was omitted in the past. So let's wait and see. But Mr. Koumjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If I could just give a brief comment, I'm moving to exclude this, and I never think that if something is relevant, that the Prosecution is going to make a motion to exclude it. It's a question of preparation. And I would just, and perhaps we can finish with this today, but if I could just comment on counsel's remark about the difference in resources and the ability to meet with witnesses. In fact, the Defence has investigators as the Prosecution does. They have the advantage that their investigators live in Prijedor, unlike ours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think we shouldn't discuss this in depth. I know the advantages and disadvantages of Defence counsel. Normally, the Defence knows better what has happened in the past and is closer to the truth because there's a good relationship to the client. And on the other hand, we shouldn't discuss in-depth all the capacities the OTP has. This is not a matter we should discuss here and today and are wasting time by doing so. Therefore, I would kindly ask the usher really now to escort the witness into the courtroom. Thank you. Please distribute the provisionally marked exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would you please be so kind and give us your solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, the witness is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mrs. Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just so the record is clear, my name is John Ostojic, along with Branko Lukic and Danilo Cirkovic; we represent Dr. Milomir Stakic. I'm going to be asking you a series of questions here today. As we previously discussed, I'll be asking them in English. And I would ask you to please wait, although you may anticipate some of my questions, to wait until you fully hear my question before you give us an answer. Fair enough?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: For the record, can you please state your full name and spell your last name.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Ljubica K-o-v-a-c-e-v-i-c.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you please share with us your current marital status. If you're a widow, or are you currently married?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I'm a widow.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us if you have any children.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have a son.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us the name of your late husband.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: My late husband's name was Milan Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Forgive me for asking, but what is your ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I'm a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In the spring and summer of 1992, where did you reside?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: In the spring and summer of 1992, I lived in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is that within -- that's the city of Prijedor which is within the Prijedor Municipality. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Correct. In the town of Prijedor, in the municipality of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And with whom did you reside there in the spring and summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I lived with my husband and my son.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you live in a home, a house, or an apartment?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: We lived in an apartment in a neighbourhood called Raskovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you, to the best of your recollection, share with us the specific address and apartment number where you resided in the spring and summer of 1992.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I remember because I still live there. It is Zarko Zgonjanin Street, number 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In that apartment complex, can you tell us the ethnic background of your neighbours, again, for the spring and summer of 1992.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Until then, I didn't realise what their ethnic background was, but I now see that it is important, so I made an effort to find out. I just greeted them. I knew their names. There were Croats, there were Serbs. But I don't make a distinction between Croats and Serbs by their names because I am not a native of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Kovacevic, forgive me for --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Forgive me for having to ask this question again, it's just for purposes of correction, with the Court's permission. It's my understanding that you also mentioned that Muslims were living within that apartment complex in which you resided in 1992. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It just didn't appear on the transcript, and that's why I'm just asking you so that we're clear on that issue. Within your apartment complex, people resided there of all different ethnic backgrounds, Muslims, Croatians, and Serbs. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me move to your educational background if I may, can you share with us the highest level of education that you attained.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I have an associate degree. I am a defectologist.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, when did you graduate or when did you obtain your degree.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: In 1973, actually I started working in 1973, but I believe that I graduated in 1972.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Where did you obtain your degree, from what university or college?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: In Belgrade. It was a university for the education of teachers working with students with special needs.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Share with us, if you will, your employment history commencing in 1973. Where were you first employed, and then tell us the years in which you were employed there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: It was in Maglaj, a small town in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So that is when I worked in a primary school. And I worked with retarded children. I had two classes, and I worked as a special-needs teacher, teacher teaching children with special needs.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And for what period of time did you work there? From when to when?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I worked there from 1973 to 1976. And then Mico and Ljubimir and I went to Kljuc, and from there, we went to Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just so that we're clear, when you say "Mico," you mean Milan Kovacevic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: When you say "Ljubimir," you're referring to your son. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were a family.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you give me the reason why is it you and your family went to Germany in 1976?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: We lived in Kljuc. Kljuc is a small place. And I always wanted to go back to Serbia. And Germany was the way to go back to Germany. Mico had to complete his residency in order to be able to find work Belgrade. So he went to Germany to complete his residency.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters' correction: "Germany was the way to go back to Serbia."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Share with us the period of time that you and your family resided in Germany. How many years were you there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: From 1978 to 1983, I returned one year earlier because my son started school. And according to the agreement that was valid between Serbia and Germany at that time, my son should have started school in Germany, and then my husband would have had to come back. I didn't want my son to stop his education at one point, so I returned before he started school.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you become gainfully employed subsequent to your return to Yugoslavia in 1983?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but not immediately. I started working in Cirkin Polje in the institution for mentally retarded children and adolescents.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Share with us the time frame in which you were at Cirkin Polje working with the mentally retarded children and adolescents. From what period of time to what?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I don't recall the dates, but it was between 1983 and 1992. And in September of that year, I left for Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So is it fair to say that you actually were employed at that medical institution dealing with mentally retarded children and adolescents during the period of April through September 1992. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Share with us, if you will, the composition of the ethnic background of those children and adolescents that you were helping and caring for from April through September 1992.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: It was a welfare institution, a health-care institution, and an educational institution. As far as the ethnic background of the children is concerned, while we worked at that institution, we did not segregate children by their ethnic background. This information is not accessible to me. There was a nongovernmental institution from Finland who has that information, and I may have learned that at one point. But I don't remember. Even -- although I knew that this may be important today, I couldn't obtain that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you care and treat for those mentally retarded children and adolescents the same regardless of what their ethnic background would have been?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Of course. When you work in an institution like that, and if you see a child that is not capable of caring for themselves, then it doesn't occur to you what their ethnic background may be. I would have to think long and hard in order to find out what their ethnic background was. We treated everybody the same, and the only distinction we made between the children was whether they were severely handicapped or not, whether they were epileptic or not, whether they are included in the system of education, whether they are under the system of work occupation, whether they needed the attention of a third person and the full care of that third person. These were the only criteria we applied when we made a distinction amongst those kids; nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did anyone, ma'am, at any time instruct or order you to treat any of the children that you were caring for and treating any differently than you had throughout your entire career while at Cirkin Polje, from 1978 to 1983?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean, anybody? Nobody, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Continuing with your -- just to correct the record, on page 68, line 6, I limited the time period from 1979 through 1983. Looking at my notes, that was the time, I believe you testified, you were in Germany. Subsequent to that, you worked at Cirkin Polje all the way through September of 1992. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: When I returned from Germany, now you have confused me. I returned from Germany in 1983. Then I started working, and I worked until the end of September 1992 in the institution for the handicapped children and adolescents.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I apologise for causing any confusion. With the Court's permission, I'd like to re-ask that question with the correct date. Specifically up through and including 1992, did anyone, ma'am, at any time instruct or order you to treat any of the children you cared and treated, adolescents or children, while at Cirkin Polje up to and including September of 1992?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No, never, nobody.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Following September of 1992, did you once again become gainfully employed?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: After I left for Belgrade, in September of 1992, I returned in the summer of 1993. I didn't work until the year 1994, then I got employed in the centre for welfare and -- social welfare. And there I worked in the administration for the registration of refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And how long did you work with the centre for welfare and social services where you were the administrator for the registration of refugees?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I worked there from 1994 to 2000 when I was invited to go back to Cirkin Polje and work there, because they had a shortage of staff, of trained personnel. That's why I was invited to come back. I stayed there for six months, just to see whether I was still able to do that. Because it is a very difficult job. And then I felt I really couldn't do it. And after six months, I returned to the centre for welfare and social services.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Am I correct that you are still employed by the centre for welfare and social services?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I still do. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What is your job title?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Currently, the centre for social welfare, I work on the accommodation of persons with special needs. We are talking about all kinds of handicaps. We are talking about blind children, deaf children, mentally handicapped children, children with physical handicaps. That's my job. I put them up in different institutions, and family care, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me when you arrived here at The Hague. Two days ago? Four days ago? When? Or was it yesterday?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I think it was yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You arrived yesterday morning, and we had an opportunity to meet for the first time last night. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And with you, you brought a CD from the centre for welfare and social services which contains data of the registration, names, and identification numbers among other things of people, men and women, who were refugees during the period of 1991 through 1995. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With the Court's permission, I would like to direct the audiotechnician booth to place the CD that we provided them so that we could have the witness answer some questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask, you tendered an entire CD-ROM. On this CD Rom are four files. One consists of 31.594 rows, and the others are more limited. Do you tender all the four files or only the one?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We are tendering all four, Your Honour. And if I can have the Court's permission to have the usher to assist the witness to transfer the screen on a video text so that she could follow along.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And you are starting now with the first file. Correct? If we can please name the file that we know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: On the top left-hand corner, there's a connotation that is referred to as Izglav, I-z-g-l-a-v. And that is page 1, starting with the left-hand portion of the document with the numerical 1 appearing below.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This is the 1 ending with row 31.594. Right?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm being assisted with this. We think that if we turn the videotape on the computer evidence section of your screen, as opposed to the video evidence, the Court may be able to see a better picture of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I have it right now on my laptop. There is a file called Izglav, Izglint, Izmov, Izin. We start with Izglav.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just so the Court is aware and I'm informed, the document that we have which is Izglav is the main document of our exhibit. The following three disks are actually the manner in which it would assist anyone reviewing this CD in order to understand the various connotations within that first CD. The first one Izglav is the main CD here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask, "Izglav" stands for? Abbreviation for what word?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: "Glavne izbjelgice", which is mainly -- or main refugees or refugees mainly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't see anything on the screen. What is this?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Kovacevic, you're looking at a screen of one of the CDs that was given to me, which lists out the various refugees that came and travelled from various parts and portions of former Yugoslavia to the Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you understand how the columns are broken down at all? And can you explain the various columns to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, I have an objection because I'm working at a severe disadvantage since I just learned about this and it's not translated. But I'm not sure that this witness is testifying in any way from personal knowledge or what -- who it is that authored or what the circumstances are in which this data was gathered. So we are presenting completely -- information data of completely unknown sources. I would like -- if the Court is going to allow further questioning, I would like first to be able to voir dire her about her knowledge of these -- this information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think the document and the source should be identified first. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Ms. Kovacevic, while you were employed in the centre for welfare and social services, is there within that centre binders of books which maintain registration data for refugees that came within the Prijedor Municipality from 1991 through 1994 or 1995?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask counsel on this specific point not to be leading the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I would do the same and also ask --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. And also ask the witness the latest update -- is it true that the latest update of the document we have before us is the one from the 16th of February, 1976, or what is the source? When was this file produced? And by whom? And what were the underlying sources?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, with the Court's permission.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: When I first started working in the centre for social welfare in 1994, I worked on the records. That's recording the refugees and people being declared as refugees who came as refugees from all the different parts of the former Yugoslavia. So it could have been from the federation, which means the Muslim or Croat-controlled parts of Bosnia, from Croatia, or from Slovenia for that matter. While I worked there, that's my unit, I was some kind of head of that unit. Over 22.000 refugees were registered and declared as refugees. And I took part in collecting these registrations. What I can see here on the screen, this is probably a PC version of the file. I didn't really use a PC, but I did record refugees when they arrived in Prijedor. It was their obligation, as soon as they could, to go to the centre for refugees and then to the centre for welfare and social services so that they can be registered as refugees. And then in the SUP, they would get some kind of a substitute ID, which was some sort of a replacement for their passport or their original ID. And this was their new personal document, the one they should be using in their new place of residence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, I do have an objection to the relevance of a list of refugees since 1994 in the municipality of Prijedor. I don't see how the names and data regarding refugees who came to Prijedor after the indictment period is relevant to any of the allegations regarding ethnic cleansing during the indictment period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Submission by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If we ever get an opportunity to review the document, we'll see that within the document the data clearly contains refugees that came within the period immediately prior to the indictment, specifically, prior to April 30th of 1992. I think other testimony substantiated that from various witnesses, including the witnesses that the OTP called. So I think it is important, and necessary, when viewing this case in its totality to determine what effect in the Prijedor Municipality refugees that came from other areas, including Croatia and Slovenia, what effect, if any, they may have had on the Prijedor Municipality during the critical time as outlined in the indictment April through September of 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask to which column do you refer, K or L? Datum Prijave or Datum Obrade?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Datum Prijave is when they initially came in and registered, so it would, in our submission, logical that if they are registering as a refugee, that in fact at the latest point would be the date that the registration shows. But as I hope Ms. Kovacevic will testify, it came prior to that time, as she herself experienced in one other area. So that's the date that they formally registered with the centre, but it's our view, based upon what we hope the witness will testify to, that people came months prior to that and merely registered themselves during the period of time as reflected within the data. We were hoping, as the Defence always does, to give the Court the complete set of the document as it was given to us without redacting it. If the OTP feels that the 1994 refugees in that area should not be counted in the 32 or 22.000 refugees that were in the Prijedor Municipality during that time period, we will make that amendment, and we'll strike those from the record. However, this is an original CD that we got, so we left it to the Court in its original form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: After first review, we can see that the data in column K are in most cases somewhere in between 1991 and 1993. So I think we have to decide later on the probative value of this document. But I think we shouldn't waste too much time. Please introduce what the different columns mean, and then we will draw the necessary conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Kovacevic, thank you for your patience. If you can just tell us and read for us the columns as they appear, and tell us what the column itself below it, what appears before the designated title of the column.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: The first column is personal code. That was the code under which a person was registered. And members's code. I'm really not sure what this means. And family, 1, 2, 3, members, Rodic, first and last name, sex, date of birth, place of birth, municipality in which the person was born. Republic. And then 014 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]... Mention also in which column we are in the moment. So, for example --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: -- Column A, the number of registration, and B and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Kovacevic, I'll try to ask the question if you don't mind, although it will not be leading, but just so that we could all follow it. You explained the first column furthest to the left. You explained, although let's have it again, what the second column is from the left. What is that column for, which is designated as column B?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Column B, this is processed by a computer, this list. What I did, my job was to have a conversation with the refugee first, take the refugee's personal information, enter this personal information into a form that was used. But we did all of this by hand. The image I can see here, well right now I can't on the screen because it's lost. It's a computerised image, and believe me, this is the first time I see it. I never used a computer in my work. I was a specially trained -- I was a trained teacher for children with special needs.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Ms. Kovacevic, within that column B, you list three specific or -- or you identified previously three --

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I assume that column B shows 01, 02, 03. I take that to mean three family members, although it says three members, then family. Perhaps it Rodic, Rodic, Rodic. We have three members here of that family. The form that I would fill -- would be filled separately for every member of the family. Now, how it was processed by a computer, using the computer, I don't know. But I assume this to be showing the same data. May I just please explain the method we used to register the refugee. The refugee would first come to us. We would talk to the refugee. We would take his information. Enter it into special forms. Then you would draft a decision that the person has been identified as that particular person, and that the person was a refugee from whatever town the person --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]... For a better understanding of the entire document and the relevance that we can really decide on the relevance, could you please be so kind and go through column by column that we understand what this shall mean. You explained to us column A, B. And now we are on the following, column C.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. C, that is name of person registered Rodic Simo Radomir. That's father's name and last name of the person being registered as a refugee.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. And column D.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Column D, "M" means male. Column E --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think it's obvious, but "M" under column D is for male. "Z" is for female. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Column E --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could make a quick objection. The witness indicated that she has never seen this before. Why present this document through this witness who has no knowledge of its preparation or the document? We don't know who prepared this or what its reliability is. She has never seen it before.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I just add something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Before we decide on the relevance, please, continue explaining what the meaning of the certain columns are. Datum Rodjenja.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Date of birth. Column C, date of birth. Column F, place of birth. Column G, municipality where the person was born. Column H, the republic in which the municipality where the person was born is in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What -- sorry to interrupt. What does it mean is in? At what time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. That's not what I mean. Can you just put the image back as it was. A certain person was born, for example, on 3rd of June, 1939. The village where the person was born was Kriva Rijeka, the municipality was Bosanska Dubica. Bosanska Dubica is in Bosnia and Herzegovina. That was the republic. That's what these columns mean, F, G, H. It's all about the place of birth.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you please proceed with the next column, I.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Column I and J, I'm not sure what these two mean. These might be computer marks. Now, let me tell you the following: I didn't use a computer. But the forms we used, those forms were processed, electronically processed, contained the following information: Profession, education, level of education, current job, and the corresponding codes were entered. So the form didn't say married, it had a special code for that, 14. So every code had a special meaning. A person was a doctor, for example, single, or unemployed, the level of the person's education with the corresponding codes. And when forms were entered into a computer, these codes were used.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may, to assist the Court and the OTP, the other disks clearly identify the number --

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Here, have a look.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But I think we can abbreviate this procedure.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The indicator, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Isn't it true that we are discussing here people living under a new address later in Prijedor and coming from a former address as we can see it mostly from Zagreb, in most cases? When we go further on, the column -- I can't see here on my laptop. Could we see the following columns after O, P. Could you please go to this side and further on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Further, further, further, further. Here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This was the previous address where the person lived beforehand. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, that's correct. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And then continue further, further. And then we see another address.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the new address where the person is currently registered as living. That's inside Prijedor, after reaching Prijedor from Zagreb or wherever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So then, may I now hear from the Defence, what is the relevance to know that people came from other countries -- from other towns or regions to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The Defence believes that it's extremely relevant for two reasons, Your Honour: One, witnesses from the OTP testified that there was an "atmosphere of fear" that was within the Prijedor municipality. I think witnesses should be allowed to testify as to what effect, if any, refugees came from a war-torn area who were kicked out and moved into the Prijedor Municipality, what if any effect that had on Prijedor as a municipality and on its people. Likewise, we believe that some of the pressures exerted from individuals who claim or were at that time identified as refugees, what if any pressure did they exert to people who they considered were perpetrators of crimes against them. For those two reasons, we believe that when witnesses testify about atmosphere of fear and how the events in Prijedor transpired, and when we discuss things such as a plan or a conspiracy of some kind in a specific municipality, the Defence strongly believes that it should be taken in context. And when you introduce a foreign object or people outside of a municipality to a new municipality, we believe that it would cause some disruption at the very least. And unfortunately, can result in some graver or a graver situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask a final question in this context, to

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Did you also include what was the ethnicity of those people coming, in this case apparently, mostly from Zagreb and then going to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the information is entered, of course, you ask the person about the person's ethnic background. In 99 per cent of the cases, the people who came were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We just now put on the screen one of the tapes which is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We just placed on the video monitor one of the tapes which has "IZIND" in the top left corner, and if I may just ask the witness, although that's within the CDs that were provided to the Court and the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you just tell me what the screen before you, what does it mean? Is that the indicator of the various ethnic backgrounds, so that when you go back, you can look at the code and determine which person was of which ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's the indicator I was talking about. I didn't know what it meant at first, 01 probably means that the person is a Serb. 02 probably Croat. And 03, Muslim. 04, others. And then you have other codes and indicators following, housewife; occupation; health insurance; where the person resides, with parents or in an abandoned house. Then what sort of assistance or subsidies is the person receiving in kind. 03, whether the person has anywhere to live in Prijedor, whether the person has a place of residence in Prijedor. 04, whether the person was put up in a special home. 05, whether the person received any assistance in terms of clothing. And then 103, whether the person lives in the person's own house. 104, whether the person is using social housing. 002, level of education. A PK worker or an NK worker, and then student or child and so on and so forth. So these are the codes that I couldn't recognise a while ago because we didn't have these specific codes on the forms that we were using, because when we were using those forms we only entered the information which would then be forwarded to the SUP where it would then be processed on a computer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Now we can hear the final arguments by the parties on the relevance of these documents. When you have a glance on the ethnicity, you will find out that 99 per cent were, in fact, Serbs. I could identify 3 Croats. No Muslim. So could be the purpose of discussing the immigration of Serbs to Prijedor? And it's open for both parties to comment on the relevance, and then we will decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I can maybe cut it short, because I'm not objecting. I don't think it hurts me. I would make a couple suggestions. One, that because this is going to create huge problems if we ask to translate this entire document, I think it is of marginal value that only the heading be translated. And secondly, that it be marked confidential because it has person's addresses.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I only disagree with the OTP that it has any marginal effect, and I also take exception that they think it doesn't hurts them. It's not a question of hurt or help. It's a question of getting to the truth. They knew this information as well and they could have brought this information forward, as they did other information. I do agree with their suggestion, however, that when this does get translated, although I thought we pretty much covered all the significant parts, that the translators do confine themselves to the categories and the columns and the various indicators that were within the CDs. But I do think that this is of extreme value to all the parties in the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I won't comment on Mr. Ostojic's comment that we knew about this and could have gotten it ourselves. It arrived today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think...

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: May I add one comment -- actually, we join in asking this to come into evidence. We think the fact that such detailed Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. records of individuals coming into the municipality does have relevance to our allegations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I don't want to comment on this. But I think following our deliberations, this document is as such admitted into evidence. But it need not be commented today by the witness before us because it's, in the way it's built up, self-explanatory. If only the witness could tell us a little bit more on the group of persons she, together with others, interviewed and that formed the basis for this. And then later on, we can use the CD-ROM as such without any further translation. And then it should be treated as a sealed exhibit because, no doubt, there are personal data included, and I'm -- to be honest, I'm surprised that we receive these documents under data protection law of some countries, this would not be admissible. But we have it now before us, but it has to be strictly under seal. So therefore, admitted into evidence as D43 under seal. And we need no translation and no further explanation save related to the source. And if you then please continue with the testimony of the witness before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Kovacevic. If you heard the Court's comment and suggestion, I think we need to know if you could tell us a little bit more on the group of persons that you, together with others, interviewed, and that which formed the basis for the material that we reviewed here.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I have already said that I started working with the registration of refugees in 1994, and I can say that I worked there in 1994, 1995, and 1996. This may seem a bit odd, but it is true, and I also worked there in 1997. Why were the refugees registered for such a long time? Firstly, a refugee who came to us in 1995, their number was so huge that we couldn't register all of them. We registered a hundred every day, and they waited in front of our doors for days and nights. They waited their turn to get their refugee identification papers. When they received their refugee identification papers, that meant everything to them. It was the proof of who they were. Based on those registration papers, they could obtain health care, they could go to seek medical services. And based on that document, they were entitled to humanitarian aid. Bearing in mind that all these peoples did not have any money or any other means for life, they had to be provided for, and the refugee identification paper was just the beginning of their way to deal with all the other questions. It was not a small group of people. We are talking about thousands upon thousands of people. Between 1994 and 1997, we registered 22.000 people. We talked to everybody. We took their personal data, and we tried to help them with dealing with their problems in Prijedor. That was my role, mine, and the role of the other three people who worked with me. So I tried to help them to solve their essential problems once they reached Prijedor from other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I do have two more questions on the effect of refugees, if I may, unless the Court feels that I should strictly move to another area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We continue for another five minutes to the next break for a quarter of an hour. But that we really can understand it, you registered these 22.000, if not more, people, 99 per cent Serbs, coming to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask you, why did you register primarily 99 per cent Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid I have been misunderstood. We registered everybody, all the refugees who reported to us during that period of time. But 99 per cent of them were Serbs. There were also Muslims who fled from Croatia and settled in the federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. But the national composition of the refugees was as such. There were 99 per cent of Serbs, and there were 1 per cent of other ethnicities. But we registered everybody who reported to us as refugees. In order to prove to us that they were refugees, they had to show to us a document proving that they fled from a certain place. Either an identification document or a passport, any proof that they used to live in the place from which they fled. We took any such document as proof that they are indeed refugees from somewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And also, for a better understanding, you mentioned the number of 22.000 people. If I compare with the CD-ROM provided by you, it ends with 31.594. And as you indicated beforehand, it's reflecting not only the number of persons, but also the families. So all in all, it would be more than 31.594 persons coming to Prijedor. And among them, about 99.9 Serbs. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] More or less that would be that. But I also said that I started working in 1994. The registration of refugees started even before that. And that job was done by other people. Ever since I came over, about 22.000 refugees were registered. There were even more refugees than that, but in order for them to register with us, they had to show us some proof of their refugee status. If they didn't have any document to prove their refugee status, we couldn't register them. So there were even more than that, even more than that number that I've mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. If you continue for about five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Kovacevic. Just quickly, I want you to focus on the time period prior to April 30th of 1992 for my following couple questions. Was there, ma'am -- I know you didn't work at the centre for welfare and social services in 1992, but was there an influx of refugees that came from other republics or other areas into Prijedor Municipality prior to April of 1992 that you yourself personally observed and experienced?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: In 1992, I worked in Cirkin Polje. Refugees started coming to Prijedor already in 1991. How did I know that? We started seeing a lot more people in the streets than usually. Then I talked to people in my workplace and my colleague every now and then would tell me, my brother and his wife came from Zagreb with their children. The house is crowded. That's how I learned that refugees started arriving from Zagreb. But not only from Zagreb, but from all over Croatia. A small number also came from Slovenia. When I talked about the way they lived, they told me, they go to the Red Cross to be registered for humanitarian aid. And then also, there was also evidence to be seen in the hospitals, in the health centre, because in the waiting rooms, people tend to talk amongst each other. That's one part of the story. Secondly, when I worked at the social welfare and services centre, they would come to us for various reasons, not only for the ID papers, but also when they wanted to enroll children at school, when they wanted to change their address. For example, they came from Zagreb or somewhere else in Croatia, and they lived with their parents. And then they found a place of their own. In order to be registered at the new address, they had to come to us first so that we could register the change of their residence. So while I worked in that job, I spoke to the refugees, and they would give me the entire history of where they came from, when they came from, so I could build a picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just briefly one last question, if I may, on this issue, so that we can take our break, Mrs. Kovacevic, to the best of your recollection, what effect did the influx of these refugees from Slovenia or Croatia have on the general municipality of Prijedor? If you noticed any, please share with us that which you noticed and experienced.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Of course it had an effect on Prijedor, primarily a psychological effect. Refugees were a novelty to us. The notion of somebody being a refugee was new. And the situation that they flew from was also new. It was a psychological burden for all people because everybody realised that they could find themselves in a similar situation to have to flee the place where they lived, that one could lose their job, that one could lose their house, that one could lose their life. That was a psychological burden that had a huge effect on me personally, because I realised that war was a reality. The second effect was the economic effect on the town of Prijedor. The situation was difficult. Even before that, there was a huge number of unemployed people. There was a high level of poverty. There were a lot of beggars on the streets. That was the second type of burden. These people had to be provided for. They had to be provided with food, with clothes, because they came barefoot and barehanded. Some people had nothing but plastic bags in their hands. Some of them, in order to flee Croatia, they just had to pretend that they went to do some shopping. That's why they had plastic bags in their hands. As a matter of fact, they didn't go shopping. They fled their houses in order to save their hides. I don't know whether the following information is relevant or not, but one of the persons working with me on the registration of refugees was Mrs. Ljiljana Babic who came from Zagreb and who told me a lot about what was going on there. And she told a story about how she fled together with her husband, how the two of them had fled Zagreb. Therefore, I can tell you that I was quite familiar with all of these problems. I heard from the people that I worked with as well as from the people that I had to see in my official capacity. It was a great fortune that the situation was rather peaceful in Prijedor so that the municipal government could accept these people and provide for them, organise their accommodation. It was -- I'm talking about the year 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, that's all I have on this issue, with the Court's permission, and I think it's a good time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's time for a break. But at the same time, the Trial Chamber takes the opportunity to ask the Defence to concentrate on that what we could read on the proffer. And due to the shortage of time, we would ask you to conclude your examination-in-chief within the next 30 minutes after the break. The trial stays adjourned until 5 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon once again, Mrs. Kovacevic. I'm going to proceed. I apologise for the confusion that I may have caused with respect to the tape. I'd like now to turn our attention and focus on a couple of different areas. And with all due respect, I would like you, if you can, to describe for us your late husband Milan Kovacevic. Tell us the type of person and individual that he was.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: My late husband, first and foremost, he was my husband, the father of my son. He was a doctor. As a husband, he was the Balkan-type husband. He looked after his wife, making sure she had enough to eat and a roof over her head, making sure she was protected if attacked. He never brought me flowers. He never gave me any special presents for the Mother's Day, but I think he respected me, and I think he loved me. He loved all people. He was a humanist, and people liked him. He was an exceptional father, unlike me as a mother. Sometimes I yelled at my son; sometimes I even hit him. He never as much as raised his voice. He never complained about anything, even if his son was about to fail in five different subjects in school. He never said anything. And my son got some stick from me for that. And Milan asked him, How many subjects are you about to fail? He said, Five, dad. And he gave him a hundred German marks for each of the subjects totalling to 500 altogether. And he said, You have to pass all these subjects. And in a month, as a matter of fact, he did. And he told me, You're supposed to be trained to deal with kids, and I'm a doctor, but obviously I'm better at these things than you are. As a man, he was good in almost in almost everything, and I often used to tell him, complain to him, that he was a better man to other people sometimes than he was to me. He did a lot of good to other people. He told me once when I had a problem that his personal motto, his slogan, was help whoever you can, but never do anyone any harm. You choose a man to spend the rest of your life with. What do you think about them? You think about if he's a good person, if he's employed or unemployed. But when I met him as a man, I realised that what I really loved about him is that he had a deep feeling for the common man, for the small man, and he had an instinct to protect people who weren't well enough. And he had a great instinct to shield people who were suffering, maybe that was because a doctor by profession. Now speaking of my family or speaking of other people, unrelated people even, he always had this instinct to help people, he would always help people any which way he could. I keep meeting people, even today, who thank me for what Mico once did for them, for his help in receiving people to hospital to be treated and in treating them the right way. Sometimes, he was on duty even when he wasn't required to be just because someone asked him to. I spent over 28 years of my life with this man. I could talk about him for a very long time. He was a very honest person. That's a character trait that I respected very much in him. He was not a materialist. He didn't care about very small things in life. He was a flexible person, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I may, Mrs. Kovacevic, specifically over those 28 years, but primarily within the period of 1992, did you ever observe or see whether Dr. Kovacevic ever exhibited any ill will or hatred against Muslims or Croats?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: During the 28 years that we spent together, not a single time. Really, not a single time. I never noticed Milan distinguishing on a national basis. He tried to look for the person and see if the person was a good person or a bad person. We discussed people sometimes, and I used to criticise people. And he would always tell me, Well, what right do you have to criticise other people? That's what he always told me. And that's exactly how he was himself. He refrained from judging people and from criticising people. I think he had more friends where he worked, colleagues, Muslims and Croats, than Serbs. He was close friends with the Resic brothers. He didn't talk that much about his job at home. It was just the sort of man he was. Once he was home, he stopped thinking about his job. He was home finally, and his job was never discussed at home. He would leave his problems behind. If he did say anything, and whenever he talked about, he would talk about the Resic brothers. If there was an operation, usually these two brothers sometimes would have an argument assisting him during the operation, and Mico was always the one to calm them down and to bring peace between them. When he was the manager of the hospital, there were a lot of people working there. But mostly non-Serbs, I would say, accounted for the majority of the hospital's employees.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Specifically in the time period of 1992, share with us if you will whether Milan Kovacevic discussed with you the political situation in Prijedor and whether he thought that a peaceful solution with all ethnic groups could be reached.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: As I said, Mico never discussed his work at home. He did not want to give me additional burdens and worries. But I was the one who asked the question. I said, Mico, what's happening? Is it possible that a conflict will occur? However, I must say something before I go on. After the elections, he wasn't thinking about going into politics. There were certain pressures, though, and then he agreed. But he was absolutely enthusiastic about the way the Serbs, Muslims, and Croats cooperated and the way positions were distributed among the three different ethnic groups. He said they found it easy to agree on everything because it was now finally multiparty system and people expected problems to arise. However, at the beginning, at the initial stage, everything was running very smoothly. I was even surprised by the degree of tolerance that was manifest. And everything worked smoothly. You could even feel it, the way people communicated with each other. One piece of information I'd like to share with you, he came to me once. He said: "Is there a suit in our house?" I asked him, "What, you're getting married again?" I was joking. And he said, "No, I've just been invited by Mr. Cehajic to celebrate Bajram with him." So he dressed up and left for Kozarac. That was back in 1991. When he came back, I asked him, "So, how was it?" And he said, "Well, it was really, really fine. I had a very fine time."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Was Milan Kovacevic a man who advocated war or peace throughout the period of time that you knew him?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: As a man, he never had a single quarrel with anyone. He would always tell me, the only quarrels I have had in my life were with you. And I would always tell him, well I'm the only person you're married to. You're not married to anyone else I hope. He simply avoided conflict, even verbal conflict. He would never -- he would always back down even if the altercation threatened to become sharper. He would always just withdraw himself, and he was -- he kept avoiding conflict with other people. He was a very -- he was a person who didn't like conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Moving in the period from April 30th through approximately May 30th --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction, there was not a single person in Prijedor with whom he ever entered into a conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Moving to the period from the 30th of April, approximately, through the 30th of May, 1992, can you tell us the nature and extent of any influence that Milan Kovacevic had on the town of Prijedor during the summer and spring of 1992, and specifically because of our time constraints, I'm going to direct you to a conversation that you shared with me which included Eso Sadikovic. What influence, if any, did Dr. Kovacevic have at that time period?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: As I've pointed out, whatever Mico was doing, and I could see that he was always making an honest effort, he really tried hard to keep the relationship between Muslims and Croats, which I think were reflected more among the people than at government level. He tried to keep the relationship smooth. I would always ask him the same question, Mico, what's going on? What's going to happen. He would always tell me, It's all going to be fine. Just wait and see. We're working on it. No one wants to have a war. I asked for my own sake, because if there was to be a war, I thought I would just leave and go back to Serbia. However, Mico was convinced that the war wouldn't happen. He was totally convinced. He would always say, these people are reasonable. We're all reasonable people. There must be a way for us to find a solution to reach an agreement. He used to tell me all these things. So I listened to him, and then whenever I socialised with other people, I could see that there were divisions, that people started grouping in terms of their ethnic backgrounds, even at work. He kept telling me everything would be all right. But somehow I just couldn't bring myself to believe it. I thought he didn't have enough insight into what was happening among the common people at the time. But still, he was totally convinced that on both sides, people would find a way to reach an agreement and to smooth out the differences. I remember we were on our way back from the village, and we were standing outside the village after the takeover. Eso Sadikovic arrived, and Mico was very fond of this man, because they were alike. They were people who had a lot of things in common. So Sadikovic came up to Mico and said, I'll try to quote him: "You know, those idiots of mine over there in that village, those fools - I'm not from that area, so I didn't remember the name of the village - they are creating problems again. They set up a barricade. Let's just go there and talk to these people for God's sake." Mico, without saying a single word, joined Eso. They drove there in a jeep. They stayed there for a long time. It was almost midnight, and Mico still hadn't come back. I was already scared, because I did hear a number of things about Eso, a number of things were being said about him. I wasn't sure, but I had seen him before with other Muslims who insisted on ethnic divisions at the time. And with Mico, the sort of person that Mico believed Eso Sadikovic to be was not exactly how he struck me. But I said okay, if Mico had faith in him, then it must be all right. And just before midnight, he came back home. And I said, What did you do there? And he said, Well, we sat down with those people, we talked to them. We had brandy together, and that's how the whole thing ended. So this was still a period when Mico could keep certain things under control.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Eso Sadikovic was of what ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I think he was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Staying with the theme of influence, did there come at any time a request from you, ma'am, to your husband to provide any type of security within the apartment complex in which you lived? And if so, what, if any, influence did Milan Kovacevic have to provide any such protection or security?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: As I've said before, in our building, we had both Croats and Muslims, families, people who lived there, and Serbs, too. That was after the takeover. Military-aged Serbs at that time were probably somewhere on the front line. I didn't know where exactly. But they weren't in their flats. So the only people left in the building were elderly people and children, as well as Muslims who were not members of any army. They were not organised in the military way. I always felt an outsider there. I wasn't from the area, so I didn't even know which villages were Muslim villages and I didn't have any idea about that. They told me that Draskovic was a Muslim village, so I pleaded with Mico because I was afraid. Mico was a politician, he was likely to be a target of someone's revolt or resentment or someone's ethnic resentment. I was afraid I wouldn't let him go there. I said: "Mico, please, can you just make sure one thing. I would like to have a police officer pass by sort of every once in a while to just have a look just to be safe." Because there was no police in that part of town. Not a single police officer. So the windows of my flat faced both sides of the street. So I was looking through my window and I could see that outside, Muslims assembled in two groups, and I thought they would head for the building. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. I was scared, so I asked him to arrange for a police officer to just patrol the area, maybe pass by every once in a while. And he replied: "I'm not the one who decides where police officers should be." And I said, Well, Mico, at least you can look into the matter. You can see who is in the charge. I'm not asking for a special police officer to be assigned to my building, but at least I need to know that I have someone to speak in case anything should happen. And he said, "No, I just can't do that." And I was angry with him. I said, "What are you doing?" He said, "I'm trying to keep the worms from eating you up." He said, "I'm making sure you have enough to eat, you have enough to drink. But I can't be around all time, and I can't arrange for someone to keep watch over you the whole time."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just moving quickly along if I may based on the time constraints, I'm going to ask you if you can, ma'am, to describe for us the relationship if you know between Dr. Kovacevic and Simo Drljaca in the spring and summer of 1992. Specifically, I would like to know whether you formed an impression as to whether or not during that time period, spring and summer of 1992, Dr. Kovacevic was a superior to and could order Simo Drljaca to perform any or certain tasks. Share with us please your impression by first telling us what the relationship was and whether or not Dr. Kovacevic could influence any request or order to Simo Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: As I've said before, Mico didn't really talk about his work. I had information, I was aware that Simo Drljaca was the head of the SUP. What their personal relationship was between, I mean between the two of them or professional relationship, I really don't know. I only met Simo Drljaca once. And this meeting may have taken place in May or June, but I really can't remember. Because there were too many things at the same time. So many things happening. I really --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Pardon me. May or June of what year, and then I would ask you just to slow down a little bit so the interpreters can catch what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: All right. That was in 1992. I went to our cottage, which was about 10 kilometres from Prijedor. It was in the afternoon, because I worked the morning shift. I left in the afternoon, and I saw Mico and Simo. Mico was lying on the grass, and Simo was standing there, which means that he only just got there or perhaps he had been about to leave. I said hello, I greeted them, and that was my first meeting with Simo Drljaca. I did see him occasionally out in the street, but that was when we were actually introduced. We said hi, we had a chat. And then Mico stood up and offered to brew some coffee for us. I said no matter, Well, no matter. I'll make some coffee and you just stay here and talk to Simo. At that moment, I used this meeting with Simo to ask him several questions about events in Prijedor that really bothered me. At that time, I'm talking about June, this was after the events in Kozarac, I noticed that people did nothing else but just carry other people's things about the town. They were loading other things on to cars and lorries. They were driving other people's cars. And I asked Simo Drljaca: "Mr. Drljaca, will you do anything to put a stop to all this crime?" And he said: "That will be difficult." And then Mico came back with coffee, and he said in passing: "Can you imagine what happened the other day? I received word from Kozarac that a convoy of tractors and lorries was headed our way. And I sent a patrol out to intercept them. They opened fire. What could I do? I told my policemen to withdraw, to go back." And I told him, "Well, this is not a solution. If you had managed to catch a single Serb who was stealing other people's things and hanged him right here outside for everyone to see him, I don't think it would occur to anyone again to do anything like that." And then he told me, "Well, soon, there will be more Serbs in Keraterm, if they keep on going like this, than Muslims. They will soon outnumber the Muslims there in Keraterm." At that moment, I realised that even he wasn't really able to put a stop to this. I thought that was just down to people's particular behaviour. That was in connection with that particular meeting we had. I never saw Simo again. But the impression I got then, and it stayed with me later, I thought it was important. First and foremost, Simo was considered a brave man. He was good looking. He was tall. But one thing I couldn't help noticing, Mico didn't really like him at all. And I asked Mico, "Why don't you like him? Because he better looking and taller than you?" And Mico was really angry. He had to reply to begin with. He said: "This Simo, this Simo you like so much, he once pulled a gun at me." Why and under what circumstances exactly Mico never told me. But I did notice that he wasn't particularly fond of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may, again, I'm not sure if I can just have a few more minutes to proceed. Thank you. I'm going to move to another area, although we can discuss and I'm sure we'll have an opportunity to share some other views in connection with your impressions of individuals. Can you tell in respect to Dr. Milomir Stakic, do you know him?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Stakic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know Dr. Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you share with us, ma'am, when is the first time that you personally met with Dr. Milomir Stakic or when you were first introduced to him?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: The first time I saw Dr. Stakic was at the funeral of my husband's mother. That was in September of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us if at any time, from April through September of 1992, whether or not Dr. Stakic ever had attended any meetings at your home with Dr. Kovacevic that you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Maybe I didn't tell you, but I will. Mico did not like anybody coming to our house. Very few people were allowed to our house. There were usually people from his early childhood. His business associates rarely came. When he worked as a doctor, and one of his fellow doctors came, because they needed to ask him something, he wouldn't let them in. He would rather put something on and go out to meet with that person. Throughout all that time, I don't think that Dr. Stakic was ever in our house.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Share with us, if you will, Dr. Kovacevic's view or thoughts and impressions of Dr. Stakic, if Dr. Kovacevic ever shared them with you, and tell us, if you will, what he thought of him.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Mico was a man of few words, and his actions spoke louder than his words. But I know that he liked Dr. Stakic. He referred to him as a kid or "curle." "Curle" is an expression that stands for a young, gullible, honest, a person of integrity, or something like that. A person who needs to learn. I knew that he liked Dr. Stakic. He liked to hang out with him. He liked to go to his house in the countryside. Mico did not have parents, but they would go to his parents' house. And Mico also liked to go to Dr. Stakic's house. Dr. Stakic had two children, and my husband liked young children. And I believe that Dr. Stakic's company was pleasant for Mico. And if Mico socialised with somebody, that meant that he respected him for his human qualities. And if my husband respected somebody, that meant that that person was educated, that he could talk to him. At home, Mico did not discuss politics at all. We could talk about a lot of things, but never politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just for the record, I'm having some assistance. I don't think the word humanitarian was translated. But I think the witness said "humanista" to the extent that it may be of any assistance. Finally if I may with the time period, can you share or tell me specifically and concretely whether Dr. Kovacevic ever exhibited any discriminatory intent against Muslims who were living with him in the Prijedor municipality or Croatians who likewise were living and working with him in the Prijedor Municipality, at any time but also including the spring and summer of 1992.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Not only did he not express any such intents, but he made everything possible to avoid conflict. I felt sorry at times for him. We lived in Germany. We knew the meaning of true democracy. And he really couldn't understand how it was possible that two normal people living in the 20th century couldn't agree on things in a peaceful way. He would always say: "We will reach an agreement." He told me: "I have problems with Mujadzic, but I don't know. He may be getting instructions from God knows where. Cehajic and I get on well. We will agree, and we agree on something." And on the following day, he changes his mind. And I believe that he is under the influence of Mujadzic.
