I'm sorry that I don't have the time, and the circumstances are such, to show you how much effort he invested in order to avoid the conflict and the final outcome of the situation. I remember when the Serbs took over, he was very unhappy. He was a very unhappy man. He was so unhappy that it hadn't happened in the way it was agreed. He was not a stupid man, you know. He knew that a moment would come when tensions would be hard to control. And Mico would often tell me: "You may try as hard as you want to up on the top, but people are frustrated. There's a huge division among people in the situation of the economic crisis. People are hungry." And then all the images that were conveyed to us from Croatia. Whatever happened in Croatia, the refugees from Croatia created such a tension and such a division among people that I, as a Serb from Serbia, had huge problems. Being from Serbia is even worse than being a Serb from Bosnia. In the eyes of Muslims, it is even worse. That is something that I have -- I forgot to tell you. I had a neighbour who lived one floor above me. He was Muslim. And he came to me and told me that it would be best for me if I didn't live there with my son because there's another Muslim who has an order to evacuate, to kill us, to strangle us with a piece of wire. That's why I asked my husband to arrange for a policeman to patrol down the street every now and then. And then when he told me that he couldn't do that, I realised that he was really not in the position to do that, and then we left to -- for Urije to live there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a couple more, if I may.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is just a story that I have just remembered, an anecdote.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, I would just like to ask you, Mrs. Kovacevic, if you were able to during the time of the spring and summer of 1992 to observe whether or not Dr. Kovacevic could influence, control, direct, or order the army or military men to perform certain tasks in the Prijedor municipality? Was he able to do that or not?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know. I'm a layperson as far as politics and -- or political organisations are concerned. However, the military and the police never were influenced or could be influenced by the civilian authorities. To my mind, the army is something that did not belong to everyday life. We, as laypersons, did not know anything about its functioning and its organisation. So the military is something that was always separated from the civilian authorities. The police, during the socialist times and later on, as far as I know, and as far as I could see in terms of what Mico could order the army -- I don't know whether the president of the state could issue any orders to the army, but Mico certainly couldn't. The police also had its own organisation. And the president of the municipality couldn't issue orders to the policemen in the street, let alone to a higher-ranking police officer. I was present when a policeman stopped Mico on the street and asked him for his driving license and traffic license. Mico, mind you, had not done anything to deserve that. He was just pulled over, and the policeman asked him for his ID and for his driving license. If Mico had been any authority in the eyes of the police, then I'm sure that he wouldn't have been stopped for no reason at all. So my answer is I don't think so. Not only that I don't think so, I'm absolutely convinced that he couldn't influence either the military or the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mrs. Kovacevic. I'm going to turn the floor over, although the Defence would like to address the Court outside of the witness's presence in connection with other related materials before we close today. But thank you very much on behalf of Dr. Stakic and the entire Defence team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's wait and see how long the cross-examination will take us. Maybe we will then have the possibility to ask the one or other question. But let's don't waste any time. Mandatorily, because the translators, the translating team working now, has a well-deserved weekend as of 5.00, we have to make a break at 5.00 sharp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mrs. Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In the interests of time, I'm going to go directly to questions.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You told -- you described your husband. Am I correct that your husband, Dr. Kovacevic, had many friends among Muslims, particularly his colleagues in the medical profession - you mentioned a few of those names - he was well known, he was a socialable person, he was liked -- he was outgoing, he liked to be out, and he knew many people?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many of your friends and your husband's friends of Muslim and Croat ethnicity were killed in 1992?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know. I had some girlfriends, and they are alive, as well as their husbands. And as for Mico's friends, I know that Eso Sadikovic was killed, Raskovac -- no, one of them died of natural causes. One of them is still living. Dr. Iglic still works in Prijedor. He worked throughout the war, and he was the head of the medical service throughout the war. Dr. Miljus who was a Croat was the head of a service while he was there. Dr. Petrov as well. He is still in Prijedor. All of our friends save for Eso Sadikovic are still alive. When you say "friend," I don't know what you mean. But one person can have up to three or four friends, and others are just acquaintances. And I'm talking about real friends, about the people who were our true friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you think the fact that these people were Dr. Kovacevic's true friends influenced the fact that they survived the conflict? In other words, did he save them?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: These were his true friends. If he could have saved them, he would have. A little while ago, I told you that he would say, "help people whenever you can help them. If you can't help them, at least don't do them any disservices." I'm sure that he didn't do any disservices to any of his friends. If he could in any way help them, I'm sure he did. And it is a fact that save for Eso Sadikovic, everybody else is alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In fact, your husband used to tell people that Dr. Eso Sadikovic was the only person he could joke with. They both had that irreverent sense of humor, and they both were very outgoing persons. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did your husband tell you who ordered Eso Sadikovic to be killed?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No, he never talked about unpleasant things. I could only tell by the expression on his face that he was thinking about something unpleasant. But he never talked about those things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you ever ask him who was responsible for the killing of so many persons in Prijedor in the camps, and particularly his fellow colleagues, medical doctors?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I never asked him that, to be honest. I never asked him who was responsible, because I lived in Prijedor at the time. I don't know whether you have managed to get the picture of the situation in Prijedor. I can tell you that I, as a Serb, could be killed by anybody. I found myself in a situation where two guys held me at a gunpoint, and they wanted to confiscate my car. If my friend hadn't happened to pass by, and if I hadn't given them my car, they would have killed me, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Ma'am, I'm sorry I have very limited time because we want you to be able to go home. So if you could just limit yourself to answering the specific question that I ask.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: All right, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you ever ask your husband or did he ever talk about -- I'll withdraw the question and start again. Did your husband ever express any regret for the fact that so many persons that you knew, that he knew, were killed in the camps, that large areas of Prijedor such as Kozarac and Stari Grad were destroyed, and thousands of people of non-Serb ethnicity were killed during the time that he was on the Crisis Staff and president of the Executive Board of Prijedor? Did he ever express any regrets about that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean by "expressing regrets?" He suffered tremendously for everything that happened -- that was happening in Prijedor. So much so that he never smiled. When he was at home, he never smiled. Once he came home, he told me: "This is a madhouse. We are lunatics. We are crazy people. But he didn't mean only Serbs, but everybody, that everybody had gone totally crazy and nobody could control people. And he thought that the lowest of -- the lowest human feelings surfaced, and he suffered tremendously because of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did he tell you who he felt was responsible for the killing of so many persons?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, never. Never. He never told me who was responsible. He himself found everything absolutely impossible to understand. He realised that the things have gone beyond anybody's control, and that everybody did everything they wanted to do. Not only his control, but that people could not control their own actions, that people were no longer normal. That's my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your husband knew Dr. Minka Cehajic and her husband, the former president, Muhamed Cehajic. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did your husband ever tell you who ordered the killing of Dr. -- Professor Muhamed Cehajic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not even sure that he knew that. I don't think he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did he ever tell you who was responsible for what happened to Professor Cehajic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your husband resigned his position in January of 1993 as president of the Executive Board. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: He resigned together with Dr. Stakic? They resigned together.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did your husband tell you why he left -- he and Dr. Stakic left their positions, the top civilian positions, in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I told you that in September 1992, left for Belgrade. My son was then at the fourth grade of school. That happened while I was away. And I think that my husband resigned, that it was only on the 30th of April that he was allowed to resign.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No, it was in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Let's try to clear this up quickly before the break. Your husband, I'm talking about his position as president of the Executive Board, which he assumed following the takeover on the 30th of April, 1992. Correct? And he resigned in January 1993. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct. But you misunderstood me. Yes, he did resign in January 1993, but if he hadn't been scared for his life and for the life of his family, he would have resigned in 1992 when he saw that the things that he fought for, and that was peace, democracy, and a multiparty state, that these things didn't happen. If he had been in the position to resign then, he would have resigned back then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: One final question before the break: Did your husband participate in a carefully planned takeover of Prijedor on the 30th of April in cooperation with the army and the police? Would you agree with that, that your husband participated in a carefully prepared takeover of power on the 30th of April?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree because I don't know whether he participated in the carefully prepared takeover. I don't know whether he participated. I don't know whether the takeover was carefully prepared, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stays adjourned until 5.30. And I wish a good weekend to all those having the ability to leave now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. And Mr. Koumjian, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Ma'am, I'd like to now play a tape of a radio programme and ask you if you recognise the voice of the second speaker. So if you just listen to the tape, and I will stop it after the first sentence of the second speaker and ask you if recognise his voice.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Before we do that, Your Honour, can we please have an exhibit number and a date, or what tape this is so that the Defence can follow if appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I apologise to the Court and to the Defence. The exhibit is Exhibit 91. That's the -- 91A is the English transcript; B is the B/C/S; -1 is the tape. Do Your Honours have copies? I think we have copies of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I don't think we need at the moment. It's in English as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. We have copies available if you would like. So if we can just begin. The tape is set to begin, just for Your Honours and for the Defence, at page 11, that's ERN number 00633728, the last paragraph that begins with "Reporter: This is Prijedor radio." Does the Defence need a copy, because we have extra copies?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. We will now play the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I don't know, ma'am, if you heard enough of the second speaker to identify the voice. Was that your husband, Dr. Kovacevic's voice? I'm sorry, but you have to answer out loud.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If we can now continue to play the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Stop, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In interests of time, I'm not going to play the rest of the interview. Madam, would you disagree with your -- or do you have any information that your husband was not correct when he said, "it was all very well prepared," regarding the takeover?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Do I have any comments? Is that what you're asking me? Could you repeat that question, please. You have to understand that the voice that I heard has stirred me a bit -- not the text, the voice. It has affected me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We understand that. If you need a break -- you tell us whether you can go on now or not.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I can continue. Just repeat the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your husband states very clearly in the interview that the takeover of power was well prepared. Do you have any information that would contradict him regarding that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: If that's what he said, if he said that it had been well prepared, then he had good reason to say so. I'm afraid that he didn't say that in order to satisfy a certain opinion in the surroundings according to which that went smoothly. Knowing my husband, knowing that he was -- I could say superficial in everything, he was only exhaustive in medicine, and that is what he had dedicated himself to. I personally know that he did say this. But on that evening, I personally know that he fled not to the summer house but to the orchard. I don't know whether they found him there. And he then appeared after everything. I can claim this for a fact. I don't know when the interview took place, but the reasons for which he stated this could be as follows: This all came to an end without me. This was all concluded without me. But he simply didn't manage to get out of that situation. But that it was well prepared -- well, I don't think he was a person who was capable of preparing it well. He was involved in medicine. And at one point he said, I deal with medicine. These are matters that he really did not understand. Other people perhaps prepared this, and then it seemed as if a team had prepared it. And he took the credit for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, let's go a little bit along your comments. Let me follow up a little bit on those. Your husband, was he the type of man to seek power and attempt to impose his will upon other people?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: That's not correct. Not at all. If necessary, I can explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Let me ask a follow-up question regarding that, and if you need to explain, please do so. Was he the type of person to exercise power and influence over others above him?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No, he wasn't. He never liked power -- or rather, it's not that he didn't like power, but it was something that he was not familiar with. And the reason for which he behaved in such a way -- well, I participated in his resistance to entering -- to joining the party first of all. And then when the elections were held for the executive committee, the elections for the executive committee for functions in the municipality, he was convinced that he shouldn't accept this. I was surprised when he came at 2.00 and said "I had to accept this. I did accept it. But you should know, and this was through the will of the Muslim votes. This was by -- through the Muslim votes." There weren't enough Serbs, so the Muslims voted for him. And he said: "It was due to the Muslim votes." I can understand the reasons for which he did that. I've already said that we were in Germany. At that time, Yugoslavia was a socialist state; Germany was a democratic state. That's the first democracy that I encountered and in which the ordinary man is taken care of. In socialist Yugoslavia, that was an alienated state. The state was alienated from the people and the people from the state. The reason for which Mico decided to go into power, to assume power, was probably because part of the -- his experience of democracy in Germany as a foreigner and as one who didn't know the language, he wanted to transfer this experience to Yugoslavia, to apply -- to take advantage of his experience in Germany in Yugoslavia. That was probably the reason. But as far as power is concerned, well, you know, in Prijedor, Mico assumes power, or rather he goes into his office. He would spend two hours there, and then he would have say I have had enough of this. I'm not interested in this any more. He didn't even know where he should sign a certain document, but he would call his secretary and say, "Don't give me anything that I shouldn't sign." He wouldn't even read the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you have any information as to why Dr. Stakic left the position of president of the Municipal Assembly in January 1993?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I really don't have any information about that. I don't know why Mico did that, and I don't know why Dr. Stakic did that either. As I said, I was in Serbia. And at that time, I didn't know what was happening in Prijedor. I do know that at that time, Mico was involved with the hospital in Gradacac. Towards the end of 1992, he went to the battlefield. He organised the hospital. I don't think he was involved in politics at all. I don't know when he was replaced, but he wasn't involved in politics at that time either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: At the same time that your husband and Dr. Stakic left their positions, Mr. Drljaca also resigned and left his position. Is that correct? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I really don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know if anyone ever made an attempt to replace Mr. Drljaca as a chief of police, your husband or anyone else, to have him replaced, before his resignation in January of 1993?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, look, a minute ago I said Mico couldn't have appointed Drljaca, and he couldn't have replaced him either for the same reason. I know very little about that system, but even at that time in the socialist system and during the multiparty elections, I did know that the chief of the SUP and especially of the army, which was something completely different, I knew that these people weren't appointed by municipal organs. This is what you are asking me. But there must be experts who could explain this better to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If you do not know the answer to this, please say so, but don't you know, in fact --

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, no, I really don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Let me finish the question. Thank you. Don't you know that in fact the chief of police was normally nominated by the local authorities, the local powers, and that his -- and that nomination was simply affirmed by the Ministry of the Interior, that that was the common practice in Bosnia for years?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may just interject --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's better to rephrase the question. Could you please --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I don't know. By rephrasing, I may still have an objection, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The basis of the objection is the guidelines that the Court has set for both parties. If counsel has those documents or rules or procedure that he claims, as he does, that it's merely a nomination and as he calls it affirming by the ministry, let him bring it to the witness. If he doesn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I don't think that we need discuss this now and here. The question should be rephrased because apparently, at least we are not aware of these documents. Please, rephrase your question whether or not the witness can tell us about something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Ma'am, would you disagree with testimony that we have heard in this Court, that the practice in Bosnia was that the local authorities --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Once again, may I ask you to put the question in a more neutral way, whether the witness knew about this or that. Because the testimony you're referring to may be assessed by the one in this way, and by another in another way. Therefore, to be on the safe side, please rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Madam, do you know of any instance where the local Municipal Assembly nominated a person to be the chief of police in Prijedor or any other municipality in Bosnia, and the Ministry of the Interior did not appoint the person nominated by the local Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: You have made the question so complicated. But as I said, I really don't know. I know a few things from how these things worked in the socialist system. The police is one thing, and the municipality is another thing. The army is another thing. I thought that this continued in this manner, but I really don't know anything about this matter. I know certain things from before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know, was it the case, that Mr. Drljaca was forced out of office because of a split in the SDS? And the same as Dr. Stakic was forced out, and Mr. Drljaca was forced out. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I had a slight problem. Up to now, I was listening to another voice, and now I can hear a female voice. And you are still speaking. So it wasn't very clear to me. Something wasn't very clear to me. I wasn't listening to the question. It's just the interpreter who changed. I apologise. Could you please repeat that. I was paying attention to what was happening. So I didn't hear the question at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I appreciate the fact that you're confused when a female voice is interpreting me. My question, I'll try to make it clear, is; were you aware, isn't it true, that Mr. Drljaca was forced out of his position as chief of police in January 1993 along with Dr. Stakic following a split in the SDS party?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, as I've already told you, and I'll repeat this again. In September 1992, towards the end of September, I went to Belgrade. And I stayed there until August 1993. During that period, I saw my husband, Mico Kovacevic, on two occasions. He would come to Belgrade. He was at the battlefield in the hospital all the time, and I really don't know what was happening in Prijedor. And one other thing, I think that at the time the telephones in Prijedor weren't functioning so that it was difficult to communicate with Prijedor. I really don't know what was happening then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I believe you testified that you met Dr. Stakic on limited occasions, that your husband liked to socialise with him. Did it appear to you that your husband got along well with him, and they would go out together?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: As I said, the first time I saw Dr. Stakic was at my -- at the mother of my husband's -- at my husband's mother's funeral. And then when I returned to Prijedor, that was in 1993, I would see Mr. Stakic's wife more often than Dr. Stakic himself. My husband, I know that he respected Dr. Stakic. I know that he liked him. He considered him a friend, and that means he had certain qualities that he respected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Isn't it the case that they socialised, and in fact, played billiards together on occasions?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I never said the opposite.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Did they used to go -- do you know a restaurant called Oskar or Kotpolje, excuse my pronunciation. Do you know such a restaurant?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Pale. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did your husband and Dr. Stakic used to go to that restaurant?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did Mr. Drljaca, if you know, did he also spend time with Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether Dr. Drljaca spent time with Dr. Stakic, because I wasn't in Pale when Mico and Stakic were there. All I know is that when I would ask him who he was with, he would say that he was with Stakic. My husband never played billiards. He only observed. And then they would treat him to 10 marks for observing them, and that was my pocket money.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You said that your husband did not have a good relationship with Mr. Drljaca. Do you know who in political power in Prijedor supported Mr. Drljaca?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know. But it is true to say that my husband -- it's not that he didn't like Simo. He didn't hate people. But I think that he was very disappointed. He indicated that this person wasn't someone who could -- he could be together with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I want to move to a subject that may be painful for you, and again, if you need a break or something, please, let me know. Do you recall your husband being arrested in 1997?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Is it correct that the same day that your husband was arrested, an attempt was made to arrest Mr. Drljaca, and that there was a shootout, and Mr. Drljaca was killed?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I know that that happened on the same day. First, the news came out that Mr. Drljaca was killed, and then I was informed that Mico had been taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you attend the funeral of Mr. Drljaca?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No. Let me tell you. I was free to go there, but I was expecting Mico to call me, so therefore I didn't go to the funeral. Regardless of the relationship between Drljaca and Mico, I respected Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So you do not know who spoke at Mr. Drljaca's funeral. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you ever see your husband -- excuse me. Sorry. Did you ever see Dr. Stakic, after that day where your husband was arrested and Mr. Drljaca was killed, before coming to court today?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I saw him that same day, or perhaps the following day. Everything that has to do with The Hague and with the prison was an unknown for me. I thought that the attorneys needed to be paid, and I had no money to pay them. Dr. Stakic called me to give me some confidence, first of all. And then I asked him whether I would need to pay for something, and he said: "I don't know. We'll stay in touch, and we'll see whether you need to pay anything." And then later on, I learned that there was a different system regarding that, and that if you had no money of your own, then there would be an attorney appointed by a court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Are you okay to proceed? Are you all right to proceed?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: There's no need to apologise. At that time, the day of your husband's arrest, and when Dr. Stakic called you, he was again the president of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I saw him only once, and I have already described the occasion to you. You have to understand the situation. That was immediately after Mico's arrest. There was probably some 50.000 people treading through my house. My son and I didn't leave the house for a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So would it be correct then that, aside from the telephone call you talked about, you had no further contact, no telephone calls or visits, from Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: That was not a telephone call. I went to see him in the municipal building. You misunderstood me. I don't remember saying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I misunderstood you, I'm sorry. I saw him in the Municipal Assembly building where his office was as the president. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know how long Dr. Stakic stayed in Prijedor after your husband's arrest?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: At that time, please believe me, I paid no attention, either to Dr. Stakic or to other people around me. I've already told you that for a month, my son and I did not leave the house. We had different problems regarding passport, regarding trip to The Hague. And simply on account of all of that, I was not interested in what was going on in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When you saw Dr. Stakic, did he express any concern for himself after the arrest of your husband and the killing of Mr. Drljaca? Did he express concern that he himself would be a target of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No, I went to see him for a specific reason. I went to ask him what was I to do if I needed money to pay attorneys. He was in the municipal building. I came to see him when he had a break between meeting various delegations. And that was perhaps a 5 to 10-minute meeting. Not more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did Dr. Stakic express any surprise or make any comments about the fact that SFOR had arrested your husband and had attempted to arrest Mr. Drljaca? Did he make any comments about that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Not at all. No. He was shaken by the fact that Mico had been arrested. The matter was over, and what I was interested in was how to pay for Mico's defence and how to establish contact with him. We didn't talk about the other matter that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Ma'am, I just want to move on quickly and briefly address the computer disk that you brought with you. Where did you obtain that disk from?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: This is how it was: I saw that things were not quite clear regarding that. I said that I worked on recording the names of refugees, recording their names, their personal data, which we used when they obtained the refugee IDs. Upon taking that information from them, or that information would be sent to the social work centre, to the lady who was the database clerk. I know how to use computers, but I did not work on that. This information came from the social work centre. It came from the lady that was a database clerk.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So the clerk actually gave you the CD?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And when was it that you first asked her to make you -- did you ask her to make you a copy of this information?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know much about computers. They told me that they had saved that information, and that whenever needed, a copy could be obtained. She brought this to me, and I didn't ask her whether she kept a copy for herself as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And this was something that someone asked you to bring or you yourself decided that -- to ask for a copy of this data?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No. Counsel asked me, when we had a conversation, where that information was kept. And I told him that this data was maintained by the social work centre. I believe that the refugee commissariat maintained that information as well. He didn't know that prior to my current work, I was involved in that as well. I told them that I used to be involved in that kind of work as well. But let me tell you this: In addition to the computer disk, there is a master record containing a number of recordbooks, and these were the original documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When was it that you had the conversation with counsel about the fact that these records existed?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Some 15 to 20 days ago perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Now, these records are quite detailed and they contain information throughout the war years in Bosnia, including individuals' names, their identification number, place of birth, et cetera. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, all of it. This is how it was done. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So can you tell us if even in wartime conditions, this information was obtained -- was kept, was recorded, and was maintained? That's correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. From the time when that service was established within the social work centre, which was some time in 1993, the municipality had to pass a decree providing that the records concerning displaced persons and refugees had to be kept first in the refugee commissariat, and then in the social work centre, and then it had to be transferred to SUP because they were the only ones authorised to issue personal IDs or passports. We passed a decision providing that SUP was the only organ authorised to do that, and this decision was based on the administrative procedure, meaning that we had to receive evidence concerning when the person left certain Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. area and what was that area. We had to have some proof of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us, then, if similar detailed records were kept about the identity of persons detained in the prisoner camps of Omarska, Keraterm, and Trnopolje, and the names of persons expelled from the municipality of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I don't wish to be unpleasant, but you're asking me things about which I simply don't know anything. I passed in the vicinity of Keraterm prison only. I can't tell you anything about what was going on there. I can only testify about things that I was involved in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just speaking of Keraterm, you did hear about the shooting one night, shots being heard all night long, and that many, many men were killed in one night in July in Keraterm? That was common knowledge in Prijedor, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you ever speak to Minka Cehajic about what happened to her husband?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know personally Dr. Minka Cehajic, and therefore I never talked to her.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did your husband -- forgive if I've already asked you this. But did your husband ever discuss with you what happened to Dr. Cehajic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You heard about -- is it correct you've heard about a massacre that occurred in August of a convoy leaving Prijedor and passing over Mount Vlasic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I did hear about that, but much later, after the war was over.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you ever learn where -- first, let me ask you. You did learn at some point, didn't you, that Dr. Stakic had gone underground and fled Prijedor after your husband's arrest. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me just object to the form of the question, Your Honour, and I can appreciate counsel trying to probe on these issues. But I certainly cannot appreciate him to give -- to put questions to any witness which are pure speculation, have not been substantiated by any witness, and I think truly by virtue of this witness's testimony here today, that if Dr. Stakic was fleeing and running, certainly in the immediate days of the arrest of Milan Kovacevic and the death of Simo Drljaca would have given --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I interrupt. Please no arguments now. It's correct that the question should be rephrased.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know how long Dr. Stakic stayed in Prijedor after your husband's arrest?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I truly don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What was the next thing -- after you saw him at his office, what was the next thing you learned about his whereabouts?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know when it was that I learned this, but I eventually learned that he had left for Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can I have S173, please, the colour copy. If we could put that on the ELMO, and the witness can look at it just so we can all see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Madam, is that your husband's signature that appears on the left-hand side?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If I could have the witness shown S74-1B, and S74-B, there's two pages.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, this signature resembles my husband's signature. But it should be given to experts because it looks somewhat questionable to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Actually, I withdraw that given the last answer and the fact that I see a "Za" on 74-1. Your Honour, at this time -- I'm sorry, if we could have that, please, shown. The signature line is Stakic, and then it's "Za" for the signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What am I supposed to do here?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If you can just look at the signature, you see in the bottom the signature, it says Dr. Milomir Stakic. And then, correct me if I am wrong, but appears to say "for" and then a signature. Is that the signature of Dr. Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: You know what, I'm not saying that the previous signature wasn't my husband's. As far as I can see, it looks as though a letter is missing. This resembles his signature, and it probably is his.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Ma'am, did your husband know Mrs. Plavsic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Are you asking whether my husband knew Mrs. Plavsic? I really don't know. I believe he didn't, but I can't claim. He would at least boast that he was in Mrs. Plavsic's company.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know anything, and if you don't -- you have been very good about telling us when you don't have information and when you do. Do you know anything about the relationship between Dr. Stakic and Mrs. Plavsic or Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Wait a minute, please. You mean between Dr. Stakic and Mrs. Plavsic, and Mrs. Plavsic and Karadzic? I probably misunderstood you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm trying to rush myself and asking two questions at once. Let's take it one at a time. Dr. Stakic and Mrs. Plavsic, do you know anything about their relationship, how they got along?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me just object to the form of the question --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I still would like to object to the form of the question. It's inappropriate to suggest something if there's no establishment that there even was a relationship and then to ask a witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know if Dr. Stakic knew Mrs. Plavsic? Do you know anything about their relations --

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, really, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know who it was that put Mr. Stakic back in power at the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you hear that it was Dr. Karadzic that placed Mr. Stakic back in power?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. And I don't believe that that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Were you present by any chance at the Municipal Assembly or at the meeting where Mr. Stakic was proposed as the new president?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you attend any political meetings where it was decided that Mr. Stakic would be the new president?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I was an ordinary citizen. I don't think that people could go in without being invited.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In the interview your husband said that "we set up a staff." Do you know what staff he's referring to?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Have you heard of the Crisis Staff in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have. I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Would it be correct that following the takeover on the 30th of April, the Crisis Staff assumed power?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know who took over the power, but I know that the Crisis Staff existed. Now, as to its tasks, I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your husband was a member of the Crisis Staff. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I believe he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know how often your husband attended meetings of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I only know that he never liked meetings at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just for clarification, when you mentioned the CD we received today, you told us that you received it by a data processing clerk. Is it correct that this was a clerk of the social work centre?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. And I can give the a name if necessary. I can tell you what is the name of that person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If you would be so kind.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: It is Divna. Are you following me? Her name is Divna, and she is -- what is that called? She is a data processing clerk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And in which building did you receive the CD?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: In the social work centre building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: This is how it is. May I explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's not really necessary with a view to the time. But this centre is in Prijedor. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then let me know, did you ever hear Dr. Stakic on the radio?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I really don't remember. I probably did, but what do you have in mind? In what period of time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Maybe especially during the period of the so-called takeover, we'll say April 30, 1992?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember whether it was during that period of time. It is possible that I heard an interview of his, but I don't remember. I can't claim that I never heard it, but I simply don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, what was your -- what was for you the most important issue at that day of the takeover? How did you learn about this? By whom did you learn about this?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I learned it in the morning when I turned the radio on. It was quite a shocking event for me. I think that the announcer said "radio of Republika Srpska" and then the message was that citizens should remain calm. And the voice of the announcer was such that it seems that it reverbates in my ears even to this day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But it was not Dr. Stakic making this announcement himself. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. That was a lady announcer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you discuss this -- you told us you were shocked about this. Did you discuss this event with your husband?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: After that, I did not discuss. Not the event itself. What I discussed was what was to happen after that. He thought: "All right, perhaps this could be a good event, a good development. If the previous one wasn't, perhaps this could be good." And then I thought: "Well, perhaps it won't get worse." And in view of the fact what was going on elsewhere in Bosnia, I was quite afraid that it could get to Prijedor as well. And if you think logically, you realise that Prijedor cannot be an exception. But at the same time, I believe that if intelligent people were in power there, then perhaps it could be an exception. And this is the belief that I held for quite a long time. Had I thought differently, I would have gone to Belgrade immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you ever see Dr. Stakic on television?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I think that immediately after the events in Kozarac, there was no electricity supply. We didn't have any electricity for months. I think that that was the case. I don't remember watching anything on television during that period, or I didn't watch television at all. Well, yes, that's true, there was no electricity after the month of May. I know this because we had to throw away all the food that had been kept in the freezer, and I can remember that in front of my building, as there was no electricity, we would all light fires outside. And then we would all -- all of us from the building would cook outside. If this is important for the trial, it probably is. We all used one stove, which was outside, to cook, both Serbs and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: When did you for the first time learn about the setting up of Keraterm, Omarska, Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I worked in Cirkin Polje. The road doesn't go by Keraterm, not exactly. But it's a road which is parallel to it. So I was aware of its existence. But as far as when it was established, I really don't know the date. But I was aware of the existence of Keraterm. As far as Omarska is concerned, I didn't experience Omarska in such a way. I thought that -- and I don't know why. I thought that people who were in Omarska were people who had been questioned in Keraterm. This is how I understood the situation to be. I don't know why. When it was established, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you know at that time why Keraterm and Omarska were set up?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know, but as I said -- when did I talk to Simo? As I have already said, it was probably in June. People were stealing, doing what they were doing. And at that point, he told me that they were imprisoning people. And since he also told me that they were imprisoning Serbs, I took this to mean that it was a prison for people who had broken the law somehow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You said "they were imprisoning people." Who is "they"?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I mean the police. You know, who arrests people, that's what I thought. Perhaps I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask you a totally different question. Was there any event in the family or in the life of your husband or the family of your husband in the past which threatened him and which had influenced all his life, maybe through World War II?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Mico and all children from Kozara suffered a lot in 1941. There was one event and, Your Honour, I can't lie. I don't know how to lie. The journalists falsely reported Mico having been in Jasenovac. Mico was in a camp, but never in Jasenovac. He was there in a camp with his mother and all inhabitants of that village, the village of Potkozarje. He was in a camp and he would always say: "What kind of a people are we?" Since there were three guards who were guarding 500 people. How can 500 people be afraid of 3 guards? It's true that the guards were armed, but the people quite simply didn't try to flee. He and his mother were in that camp, but his mother was probably trying to survive. The instinct for survival was putting her forward, and she managed to get out of there. Mico is no longer alive, but I wouldn't want things to be falsely represented. It's not true to say that he was in Jasenovac. It is true to say that he was in camp, that he suffered a lot -- not only Mico, but everyone, all the children suffered a lot. But he wasn't in Jasenovac. And this is the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: He suffered from the occupation by the Germans. Correct? He suffered in 1941 under the occupation by the Germans. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did. But I don't think the cause of the suffering was the German occupation. He suffered because of the overall situation, too. The NDH was there, the independent state of Croatia. The Germans were in the town. The NDH army went around the villages, rounded up the people, people would flee to Kozara. The Germans were present in the town, but Mico and his mother told me that they would have -- that they would be happy if they came across a German soldier. But if an Ustasha, and those were either Croats or Muslims, they were neighbours, it was very difficult if they came across Ustashas. That's why they fled to Kozara. And I am saying this for the sake of the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Vassylenko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: My question, how it happened that your husband, a person dedicated to medical profession and family life, became a politician and started to wear a military uniform?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: As I have already explained, he didn't want to go into politics. He was a man who was well-liked by everyone -- in fact, I can't say everyone, but many people liked him. I don't know whether it was because of the way he was or because he was a doctor and they needed him. But he was able to communicate with everyone, and he was ready to listen to anyone. As far as the fact that he wore a camouflage uniform is concerned, I haven't portrayed Mico as his wife. He had two pairs of trousers and two shirts. Perhaps that's not very important. But at the time, there was no detergent. It wasn't possible to wash clothes. They received those camouflage uniforms, and he said, "This is nice. It keeps you cool, and when it's dirty, you don't see the dirt." So he wore that for a certain period of time. At the time, everyone wore those uniforms, and then he took the uniform off. Whether it was for some other reason or because he understood that that uniform had another meaning, too, I don't know. But later on, he didn't wear it any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Was your husband respected by his colleagues in his profession?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, very much so. Look, he came from Germany where he was involved in a kind of medicine that was technically more developed, so his opinion was taken into account.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Was your husband an influential political figure in Prijedor Municipality?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: You want to know whether he was an influential political figure. I don't know. But he was too naive to be a real politician, but he did have influence. That's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Have you ever discussed the fact of existence of the camps in Prijedor Municipality with your husband?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I never discussed that with him. Well, first of all, I was aware of the existence of camps, but I didn't talk about this because I knew that he didn't know much about this. And even if I had asked him about it, he would have said that he knew nothing about it. So I quite simply didn't ask him anything about that. Perhaps it was an unpleasant subject for me, too. But as I say -- you don't have to believe me, but I really thought that these camps were prisons where people were questioned as to what had happened, how they had armed themselves, whether they had armed themselves. And that then they would be sent to Omarska. I really didn't go into the matter, but that's -- that was my understanding at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: What was your reaction to the arrest of your husband?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: What was my reaction? Well, I was surprised, I was shocked -- I don't know. After a month had passed, only then did I realise that he had really been arrested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Judge Argibay, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: I have no questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your patience, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We're almost done, Mrs. Kovacevic, just a couple questions to follow up on the questions by the Court and Mr. Koumjian. Did you have any trouble whatsoever obtaining access or finding Dr. Stakic at the Prijedor municipal building immediately after the arrest of your husband, Milan Kovacevic, in 1997?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you know, ma'am, that Dr. Stakic left the Prijedor Municipality and went to Belgrade because he was getting his specialisation in the field of medicine, in a specific area? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that. But I subsequently found out that he had gone there to get his specialisation. Later on, I was told that he had gone there and that the reason for his departure was this specialisation course. I think that I have explained this sufficiently.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The Honourable Judge Vassylenko asked you a question about your reaction to the arrest of Milan Kovacevic. Immediately subsequent to that, were you provided any aid or assistance or help by the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: To follow up on a question by Mr. Koumjian regarding the records and you having been at the centre where these records are kept, where they kept information on individuals who did not migrate into Prijedor, but left other areas because they were forced to leave, keeping those records, is there anything to your knowledge which would prevent the Office of the Prosecution with their subpoena power in order to tell a Chamber the truth or to get to the truth about a situation to have subpoenaed those same records that you brought to us? Do you know of anything that would have prevented them from being able to do that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't able to follow you quite well. I spoke the truth only. And everything else that is needed regarding these records, I can tell you that there are registry books. And in addition to that, there are three types of parallel records that can be provided to this Tribunal, and that identical to the data contained in this diskette. This is contained in those records.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I understand that. For example, some of the documents that the Prosecution was kind enough to share with you, do you know that, for example, some of those documents were subpoenaed by the Office of the Prosecution from the municipal building, the police station, the Kozarski Vjesnik building? And likewise -- likewise, they were also able to, without any hesitancy, to be able to subpoena the records from your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. But the witness can't answer these questions. These are internals of the criminal procedure, and it's not a question to be put to a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you these couple more final questions, if I may: Did you know or did you hear at any time that when there was an arrest by the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Office of the Prosecution of Milan Kovacevic and the killing of Simo Drljaca, that there was a secret indictment that no one knew about that may have been in existence against Dr. Milomir Stakic? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: A couple questions, if I may. The Honourable Judge Schomburg, president of this Chamber, asked you a question in connection with the childhood of Milan Kovacevic. And you mentioned the camp that he was in. But at any time, having been with him for 30 years approximately, did you ever feel that Dr. Kovacevic had some ill feelings towards other individuals, whether they were Muslims, Croats, or any non-Serbs, because of the experience that he had with his mother as a child? Did he ever tell you: "It's because of my youthful experience that I now, at the age of 58, would like to impose that same suffering on other individuals"?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know these facts about the camp until journalists wrote about that. When he was in prison here, I asked him about that. I said: "Mico, it is said here that you had been in Jasenovac." And then he told me that it wasn't Jasenovac, but rather a camp in the vicinity of Prijedor. So as far as the camp is concerned, he never told me that it was the camp experience that had scarred him. What he suffered as a child left no marks on him because he developed and was a successful man. And that created new-life opportunities for him. I remember well that that summer of 1992, we were getting ready to go on vacation in Cairo rather than wage war. Knowing him as a person, I don't believe that one could ever come to the conclusion that he had a difficult or tragic childhood. He was a person with a great sense of humor, with a kind heart, and one would be more likely to say that I had been in Jasenovac rather than him. He liked people. And there is something I didn't tell you. Dr. Stakic should know about this. We lived in an apartment that had 50 square metres. It was on the last floor. It had no balcony. In 1991, Mico was given an apartment, and I asked him, Well, where was that apartment? And he said I've given this apartment to somebody else. I asked him to who? And he said to Suljanovic who I believe was his deputy -- perhaps I got the name wrong, but it was somebody who was a Muslim. And then I said, Well, Mico, why did you give him an apartment when we have no proper apartment ourselves? And he said to me, Why would we need a new apartment? I simply threw the keys to the apartment to him. Perhaps this is not important, but we could prove this through other witnesses including the man who had been given this apartment. Somebody who hated Muslims would not have done that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I have one final question, if I may, with the Court's permission. You were asked several questions regarding Dr. Stakic, if you saw him on the television or heard him on the radio. I know you left the Prijedor Municipality in September of 1992, because of your son's education, and you went to Belgrade. However, during the period of September 1992, were you able to read any newspaper accounts where Dr. Stakic was critical of the police and the military? Do you know if you ever had an opportunity to review such articles?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's all I have. Thank you very much, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I have two brief questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Ma'am, am I correct that you brought the information on the computer disk at the request of Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No, not Mr. Ostojic. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And the second question: Did you ever hear Dr. Stakic, the president of the Municipal Assembly in 1997, after your husband's arrest, give any speech or any public statement to the people of Prijedor saying "I'm going to Belgrade to do a specialisation and resigning my position"?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Giving a speech about going to specialisation in Belgrade, or giving any speech? I think that I heard him give a speech in 1997 or around that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I can't see any further questions. So I have to thank you, not only for coming, but also going through this difficult line of questions. I know it must have hurt you sometimes, and we all know how difficult it is to reopen some wounds. And I hope that as soon as possible, you can overcome all this. Thank you for coming. And thank you for testifying to the best of your recollection. [Foreign language spoken]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say something, Your Honour. This was my moral duty that I have with respect to my husband, to everyone who perished during this war, and the duty I have with respect to the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you once again. May I ask the usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom. Thank you for today. You're excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Very briefly, I don't want to step over the time. But we have to clarify what will happen on Monday. Until now, we didn't receive any questions for Mr. Sivac from the side of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We have them. It's just there has never been an opportunity to share with the Court. We thought we would do it in open Court. The Court asked for it today, this morning. We had it. We can tender it now. We have a copy of -- for the OTP as well under the Court's ruling. If the usher would be kind enough --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, please. Maybe, please, distribute it. And please understand that we can't rule now on the question of whether or not these questions met the threshold indicated beforehand, and the Prosecution has also the right to comment on this. But nevertheless, I would ask the OTP to be prepared that Mr. Sivac is ready to appear on Monday afternoon 2.15. And until you are maybe disalerted. In the moment, we can't really concentrate on this and go through this line of question. In principle, we are prepared to hear Mr. Sivac. But we'll let you know the final outcome. Related to next week, you should only know that on Wednesday, we sit in the morning instead of the afternoon. On Thursday, we start now, once again, a change of the bureau meeting, we start as scheduled, but we have to stop at 6.00. Do you have any informations from the side of the Defence related to the translation of your exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We did call, and we are still waiting to hear back from them, Your Honour. It doesn't seem -- because when we leave they are already gone, we left messages during the break. We hope to accomplish that by early next week and share that with the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We come back to this immediately on Monday. What about the status of disclosure of Ms. Plavsic's interviews?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was not promised, but there was an indication that they were going to present that to us today by the end of the day. And we just don't have it yet. I would also like to make the request in connection with that if we could have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's also our desire to have as soon as possible these documents that we are prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to make a point, if we could also have them in the B/C/S version so that our client could review them. And I think the interviews were done. So I don't have to make the application later. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I don't believe that there is a B/C/S transcript. There may be actual tapes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: My understanding is that -- I just was informed that we haven't received an answer yet from the Defence of Plavsic about whether they have an objection to the interviews. We did ask to give them an opportunity to make an objection. But they are being copied now. We'll also ask for the tapes to be copied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So we can expect these documents and the tapes by Monday. Because you have seen the scheduling order, and maybe -- I don't know what will be the direction, but there are two options, either to testify after the sentencing judgement or before. And then finally, it should not be forgotten, what about the typewriting expert?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I haven't heard from him, and I will check on that. Coincidentally, I asked Ms. Karper about that this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please don't forget that this question is still open. Any other issues to be resolved today?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Not at this time, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then you should only know that it is envisaged that from 20th January, whenever we sit in the morning, we sit as from 9.30 until 5.00. Sometimes the entire day in Courtroom I, sometimes in the beginning in Courtroom II, and then later in Courtroom I to have as much as possible time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just to remind the Court, we also -- I think it's one of the four of the six individuals that we received the tapes on under Rule 68. We -- they are not cooperating in terms of coming as our witnesses. We would ask the Court, if acceptable, that the Court calls them. But I would like to sit with the Court and the OTP obviously and talk about when we can fit that in based on our schedule and the Court's. We think it's -- at least we think it's relevant --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think the time is ripe for another 65 ter (i) meeting during the next week. This really concludes now this week's hearing. I thank everybody also for the extra time, but it was really helpful for the witness had not to come for a second time to The Hague. Thank you everybody. And have a nice weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
